statement: IAS 38 requires that acquired brand names have to be amortised.
explanation: Wrong. Amortisation depends on the useful life, not on how the asset was obtained. Brand names usually have an INDEFINITE useful life (no foreseeable limit to the period they generate cash) → no amortisation, but an impairment test at least once a year. Only intangibles with a finite life (licences, patents) are amortised.

statement: Tangible assets have to be measured at fair value when using IFRS.
explanation: Wrong. After initial recognition IAS 16 offers a choice per class of assets: the COST model (cost − accumulated depreciation − impairment) or the REVALUATION model (fair value at revaluation date − subsequent depreciation/impairment). In Europe the cost model is used almost exclusively.

statement: Internally generated brand names, publishing titles and customer lists can be recognised as intangible assets if they are legally protected.
explanation: Wrong. IAS 38.63 explicitly prohibits recognising internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and similar items as assets – their cost cannot be distinguished from the cost of developing the business as a whole. Legal protection does not change this. (If ACQUIRED, e.g. in a business combination, they are recognised.)

statement: When a non-current asset does not generate cash on its own, for impairment testing it should be associated with a group of assets so that this group generates cash.
explanation: Correct. If the recoverable amount (especially the value in use) of an individual asset cannot be determined, the test is performed for the cash-generating unit (CGU): the smallest identifiable group of assets generating cash inflows largely independent of other assets (e.g. a store, a magazine title, a plant).

statement: When the recoverable amount of an asset increases after a prior-year impairment, the carrying amount has to be increased up to its historical acquisition cost.
explanation: Wrong. A reversal is required, but capped: the new carrying amount may not exceed the carrying amount that would have resulted (net of depreciation) had no impairment been recognised – i.e. depreciated cost, not historical cost. For goodwill, impairment losses can never be reversed.

statement: Research costs are always expensed, whereas development costs are capitalised when they meet the requirements of IAS 38.
explanation: Correct. Research (gaining new knowledge) → expense, because future benefits cannot be demonstrated. Development (applying research to a plan or design before commercial production) → MUST be capitalised once all IAS 38 criteria are met (technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete and use/sell, probable future economic benefits, adequate resources, reliable measurement). Amortisation starts when the product goes to market.

statement: If a rental agreement for buildings meets the definition of a lease under IFRS 16, the lessee recognises the lease payments as costs on a straight-line basis in the income statement.
explanation: Wrong. Under IFRS 16 the lessee recognises a right-of-use ASSET and a lease LIABILITY. The income statement shows DEPRECIATION of the right of use and INTEREST on the liability – not rent. Straight-line rent expense is only allowed for the optional exemptions (short-term ≤ 12 months, low-value assets ≈ USD 5,000).

statement: At the commencement date of a lease, the right-of-use asset is always equal to the lease liability.
explanation: Wrong. ROU asset = lease liability (PV of future lease payments) + lease payments made at or before commencement (less incentives) + initial direct costs + dismantling/restoration costs. In the Adams example: liability 31,597 + first payment 9,968 = ROU 41,565.

statement: Indefinite-life intangible assets and goodwill must be tested for impairment at least once a year, even without any indication of impairment.
explanation: Correct (IAS 36.10). For PPE and finite-life intangibles a test is only required when there are internal or external indications (market value decline, adverse technological/legal changes, rising interest rates, obsolescence, damage, worse performance).

statement: The recoverable amount of an asset is the lower of its fair value less costs to sell and its value in use.
explanation: Wrong – it is the HIGHER of the two. A rational entity would either sell the asset or keep using it, whichever gives more. An impairment loss is recognised only if the carrying amount exceeds this recoverable amount.

statement: An impairment loss of a CGU is first allocated to goodwill and then to the other assets pro rata to their carrying amounts.
explanation: Correct. But no individual asset may be reduced below the highest of its fair value less costs to sell, its value in use (if determinable) and zero; any excess is reallocated to the other assets.

statement: Value in use is calculated with pre-tax cash flows from continuing use and disposal of the asset, excluding financing and income tax cash flows, discounted at a pre-tax rate.
explanation: Correct. Forecasts usually cover at most five years unless longer projections are reliable; if no asset-specific rate is available, the WACC can be used as a starting point.

statement: Staff training costs incurred when a production process is robotised are added to the cost of the new machines.
explanation: Wrong. Training costs (human capital) are expensed as incurred – the entity does not control its employees' know-how. Only costs directly attributable to bringing the asset to working condition (price, transport, installation, testing) are capitalised.

statement: A contract to transport cargo on a specified ship, where the supplier operates the ship and the contract predetermines cargo and dates, is a lease.
explanation: Wrong – it is a service contract (lecture exercise 3.3). Even though the ship is identified and the customer uses substantially all its capacity, the customer does not direct HOW and FOR WHAT PURPOSE the ship is used: the supplier operates it, and cargo and dates are predetermined by the contract, not decided by the customer during the period of use.

statement: A 5-year contract for a specified ship, where the customer decides what cargo is transported and whether, when and to which ports the ship sails (within restrictions on piracy waters and hazardous cargo), is a lease even though the supplier operates the ship.
explanation: Correct (lecture exercise 3.4). Identified asset, no substitution rights, the customer obtains substantially all economic benefits and directs how and for what purpose the ship is used. The restrictions are protective rights of the supplier; operating the ship is a service component that does not prevent lease classification.

topic: IFRS 16 – right to direct use (lease test)
statement: A company leases delivery trucks for 4 years, but at the beginning of every quarter the lessor must approve the routes the trucks will travel. This is a lease.
explanation: Not a lease (exam 2024). The lessor keeps the right to decide how and for what purpose the trucks are used (it approves the routes every quarter), so the customer does not have the right to direct the use of the identified asset.

statement: A company leases vehicles for its sales force for 4 years; the vehicles must not leave the national territory and must not exceed 20,000 km per year. This is a lease.
explanation: Yes. Territory and mileage limits are protective restrictions that define the scope of use; within them the customer decides how and for what purpose the vehicles are used and obtains substantially all economic benefits.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a condition to recognise an intangible asset under IAS 38?

options.text: Identifiable
Controlled by the entity
Future economic benefits are expected and probable
Cost can be measured reliably
Legally protected by a patent

explanation: Legal protection is not required (and does not suffice for internally generated brands). For separately acquired assets the criteria are assumed to be met.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company has spent several million euros researching a vaccine. It has reached stage 3 and countries have reserved millions of doses, but marketing approval has not yet been obtained. Where are these costs recognised?

options.text: In the income statement as operating expenses
As an intangible asset
As revenue for the reserved doses
As an intangible asset and as revenue

explanation: Research costs are expensed. Without regulatory approval, the development criteria (technical feasibility, probable benefits) are not met in pharma – costs are expensed. Reservations are not revenue until the performance obligation is satisfied.

prompt: An auction house with net assets of 10 million € is acquired for 30 million €. How can the difference be explained?

options.text: Its internally generated brand was not recognised in its own balance sheet, and the rest is goodwill (reputation, know-how, synergies)
Its tangible assets were overvalued in its balance sheet
Only by goodwill – brands are never recognised separately in a business combination
The difference is an acquisition loss that the buyer expenses immediately

explanation: Internally generated brands are not recognised in the target's own balance sheet but become identifiable assets at fair value in the acquirer's PPA; the remainder is goodwill.

prompt: Equipment: invoice price $540,000, transport $26,000, installation $5,000, party celebrating the installation $300. At what amount is the equipment recognised?
explanation: Cost includes the purchase price and all costs directly attributable to bringing the asset to its location and working condition (transport, installation). The party is not necessary → expense.

prompt: When is it NOT possible to perform an individual impairment test?

options.text: When only the fair value of the asset is available
When only the value in use is available
When the recoverable amount of the asset is available
When the asset does not generate cash inflows on its own

explanation: An individual test needs the asset's recoverable amount. If either fair value less costs to sell or value in use is available, it can be compared with the carrying amount. If the asset does not generate cash inflows largely independent of other assets (e.g. a single machine on a production line, a head-office building), its value in use cannot be determined – it is then tested as part of its cash-generating unit.

prompt: What is Verma's impairment loss and the depreciation for N+1?

options.text: Impairment 40,000; depreciation N+1 = 32,000
Impairment 50,000; depreciation N+1 = 30,000
Impairment 40,000; depreciation N+1 = 40,000
No impairment

explanation: Value in use = 40,000 × 3.993 ≈ 160,000 > fair value 150,000 → recoverable amount 160,000. Impairment = 200,000 − 160,000 = 40,000 (expense). New depreciation = 160,000 / 5 = 32,000.

prompt: Kohlbuy's Pritt division (a CGU) has a carrying amount of $2,400,000 including goodwill of $900,000; its recoverable amount is $1,900,000. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The impairment loss of $500,000 is entirely allocated to goodwill, which falls to $400,000
The impairment loss of $500,000 is allocated pro rata to all assets including goodwill
The impairment loss of $500,000 is allocated to goodwill and can be reversed later if the recoverable amount rises
There is no impairment, because the goodwill exceeds the difference

explanation: Goodwill absorbs the loss first; since 500,000 < 900,000, no other asset is affected. Goodwill impairment is never reversed.

prompt: A strong impairment of a CGU follows a coup in the UTOPIA region. What is the impact on the financial statements?

options.text: Decrease in operating income and in non-current assets
Decrease in operating income and increase in financial debt
Decrease in operating income and in cash
Decrease in operating income and in current assets

explanation: An impairment is a non-cash expense reducing the carrying amount of non-current assets (goodwill, PPE). Cash and debt are not affected.

prompt: What is the total impairment loss for CGU A, and how is it allocated?

options.text: 800,000: building −100,000 (individual test) and goodwill −700,000
800,000: all to the land and building
300,000 to goodwill only
No impairment because land has gained value

explanation: Building A: recoverable amount = max(400,000; 350,000) = 400,000 < 500,000 → individual impairment 100,000. CGU A after that: 3,700,000 vs recoverable 3,000,000 → 700,000 → goodwill (1,000,000 → 300,000). Land is not written up. Total 800,000.

prompt: What is the impairment loss for CGU B and the machinery's carrying amount after impairment?
explanation: Building B: recoverable max(550,000; 500,000) = 550,000 → individual impairment 50,000. CGU: recoverable = max(2,280,000; 2,000,000) = 2,280,000 vs 2,550,000 → 270,000: goodwill 200,000 → 0, remaining 70,000 – the building cannot go below its recoverable 550,000, so machinery takes 70,000 → 1,730,000. Total 320,000.

prompt: What are the lease liability and the right-of-use asset at commencement, and the N1 expenses?

options.text: Liability 31,597; ROU 41,565; depreciation 10,391; interest 3,160
Liability 41,565; ROU 41,565; depreciation 6,928; interest 4,157
Liability 31,597; ROU 31,597; rent expense 9,968
Liability 39,872; ROU 39,872; depreciation 9,968

explanation: Liability = 9,968 × 3.169865 = 31,597 (4 future payments). ROU = 31,597 + 9,968 paid at commencement = 41,565, depreciated over the shorter of lease term (4) and useful life (6): 10,391. Interest = 10% × 31,597 = 3,160. Liability end N1 = 31,597 + 3,160 − 9,968 = 24,789.

prompt: Finchley leases an office building (fair value = PV of lease payments = 4,000,000; useful life 20 years; payment 300,000 per year on 31 December; effective rate 4.5%). Impact at 31 December of the first year?

options.text: Rent expense and cash outflow of 300,000
ROU 4,000,000, debt 4,000,000, depreciation 200,000, rent expense 300,000
ROU 3,800,000, debt 3,880,000, interest 180,000, depreciation 200,000, cash outflow 300,000
ROU 3,800,000, debt 4,000,000, depreciation 200,000, rent expense 300,000

prompt: The CEO of a highly indebted company is reassured because most investments of the year were leased, not bought. What is the impact of leasing on the financial statements?

options.text: It decreases net income and cash by the amount of the rent only
It decreases assets and cash
It increases non-current assets, decreases cash and increases financial debt
It increases non-current assets and financial debt, and decreases cash and net income

explanation: IFRS 16: ROU asset and lease liability (debt ↑), lease payments reduce cash, depreciation and interest reduce net income. Leasing is no longer off-balance-sheet financing for the lessee.

prompt: Which statement on the PRODI financing decision is NOT correct?

options.text: Both solutions show a production line/ROU of 900,000 at the end of N
The loan shows debt of 1,000,000, the lease a lease liability of 919,600
Loan: depreciation 100,000 and interest 46,500; lease: depreciation 100,000 and interest 47,600
The lease avoids any increase in financial debt

explanation: Lease liability = 1,000,000 + 4.76% × 1,000,000 (47,600) − 128,000 = 919,600. Under IFRS 16 the lease adds debt like a loan – the CFO's argument is wrong.

prompt: Which exemptions from the right-of-use model exist under IFRS 16, and for whom?

options.text: Short-term leases (12 months or less) and leases of low-value assets (≈ USD 5,000 when new) – lessee only
Short-term leases and all leases of buildings – lessee and lessor
Leases of low-value assets and leases with variable payments – lessor only
There are no exemptions – every lease is recognised as a right-of-use asset

explanation: With the exemptions, payments are expensed straight-line and disclosed. Leases of minerals/oil/gas and certain licences (films, patents) are outside IFRS 16.

prompt: What is the impairment loss on Ramon's mall at 31 December N5, and the book value at 31 December N6?

options.text: Impairment 32.08 m; book value N6 ≈ 209.2 m
Impairment 40 m; book value N6 = 202 m
Impairment 34.4 m; book value N6 ≈ 207 m
No impairment

explanation: Carrying amount = 300 − 5 × 10 = 250. Value in use = 24 × 9.08 (25 remaining years) = 217.92 > fair value 210 → recoverable 217.92. Impairment 32.08. New depreciation 217.92/25 ≈ 8.72 → N6 ≈ 209.2.

prompt: Determine and allocate the impairment losses of CGU A and CGU B at 31 December N, and state the impact on net income N.
modelAnswer:
Individual tests first (property price drop): land A: recoverable max(450,000; 500,000) = 500,000 > 300,000 → no impairment (no write-up). Building A: max(400,000; 350,000) = 400,000 < 500,000 → impairment 100,000. Building B: max(550,000; 500,000) = 550,000 < 600,000 → impairment 50,000.
CGU A: carrying amount 3,700,000 vs recoverable 3,000,000 (value in use) → 700,000, allocated to goodwill first → goodwill 300,000. After: land 300,000; building 400,000; machinery 2,000,000; goodwill 300,000 = 3,000,000.
CGU B: carrying amount 2,550,000 vs recoverable max(2,280,000; 2,000,000) = 2,280,000 → 270,000: goodwill 200,000 → 0; remaining 70,000 pro rata, but the building cannot fall below 550,000 → machinery −70,000. After: building 550,000; machinery 1,730,000; goodwill 0 = 2,280,000.
Impact on net income N: impairment losses of 800,000 + 320,000 = 1,120,000 (operating expense, non-cash).
keyPoints: Recoverable amount = higher of value in use and FV less costs to sell
Individual impairments: building A −100,000, building B −50,000

steps.title: Test the individual assets with an indication first
steps.why: IAS 36: when an asset shows an impairment indicator (drop in property prices) and its recoverable amount can be determined individually, test it alone BEFORE the CGU test. Recoverable amount = HIGHER of value in use and fair value less costs to sell.
lines: Land A: max(450,000; 500,000) = 500,000 > book value 300,000 → no impairment (no write-up above cost)

steps.title: CGU A – compare carrying amount with recoverable amount
CGU A – allocate the loss
steps.why: The loss is allocated first to goodwill, then pro rata to the other assets. 700,000 < goodwill 1,000,000, so goodwill absorbs everything.

steps.title: CGU B – compare and allocate
lines: Building already at its recoverable amount 550,000 → cannot go lower

steps.title: Impact on the financial statements N
steps.why: Impairment losses are operating expenses (non-cash). Goodwill impairment can never be reversed later.

pitfalls: Taking the LOWER of value in use and fair value less costs to sell – IAS 36 uses the HIGHER.
Writing up the land to 500,000: under the cost model no revaluation above cost.
Allocating the remaining CGU B loss pro rata to the building below its own recoverable amount (550,000).

topic: Lease vs. bank loan – impact on gearing
prompt: What do you think of the CFO's comment that leasing is better given PRODI's high gearing? Justify with the impacts on the financial statements at the end of N.
modelAnswer: The CFO is wrong under IFRS 16. Loan: PPE 1,000,000 − depreciation 100,000 = 900,000; financial debt 1,000,000; expenses: depreciation 100,000 + interest 4.65% × 1,000,000 = 46,500; cash out 46,500. Lease: right-of-use 1,000,000 − depreciation 100,000 = 900,000; lease liability 1,000,000 + interest 47,600 − 128,000 = 919,600 (financial debt); expenses: depreciation 100,000 + interest 47,600; cash out 128,000. Both solutions increase assets and financial debt similarly, so gearing deteriorates in both cases; the lease is even slightly more expensive (147,600 vs 146,500 of expenses). Only short-term or low-value leases would stay off balance sheet.
keyPoints: Lease: ROU 900,000, lease liability 919,600, depreciation 100,000 + interest 47,600
Under IFRS 16 the lease also creates financial debt
Conclusion: CFO is wrong – gearing increases in both cases

steps.title: Solution 1 – bank loan
steps.why: The machine is bought (PP&E, straight-line over 10 years); the loan is repaid in fine, so the debt stays at 1,000,000 during N.

steps.title: Solution 2 – lease under IFRS 16
steps.why: The lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability = PV of lease payments = 1,000,000. The liability is then measured at amortised cost with the effective rate.

steps.title: Answer the CFO
steps.why: Since IFRS 16 there is no off-balance-sheet operating lease for the lessee any more (exemptions only for short-term ≤ 12 months and low-value assets). Both solutions add roughly the same asset and financial debt, so gearing deteriorates in both cases; the lease is even slightly more expensive.
steps.result: The CFO is wrong: leasing does not improve gearing under IFRS 16

pitfalls: Treating the lease as a simple rent expense of 128,000 (pre-IFRS 16 thinking).
Computing lease interest on 128,000 instead of on the liability of 1,000,000.

prompt: Explain the difference between research and development costs under IAS 38 and why the distinction matters for profit.
modelAnswer: Research = original investigation to gain new knowledge (e.g. lab research for new molecules) → always expensed, because future benefits cannot be demonstrated. Development = application of research findings to a plan or design for new or substantially improved products/processes before commercial production (e.g. prototypes, pilot plants) → must be capitalised as an intangible asset once all IAS 38 criteria are met (technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete and use/sell, probable future economic benefits, adequate resources, reliable measurement). Capitalised development costs are amortised from market launch over the useful life. Hence research reduces profit immediately, capitalised development only gradually via amortisation – the R&D director's belief that all R&D is capitalised is wrong.
keyPoints: Development: apply knowledge before production → capitalise if criteria met
Name IAS 38 criteria (feasibility, benefits, resources, measurement)
Profit impact: immediate expense vs amortisation over useful life

steps.title: Research phase
steps.why: Research = original, planned investigation to gain new knowledge (e.g. lab research for new molecules). At this stage future economic benefits cannot be demonstrated.

steps.title: Development phase
steps.why: Development = applying research findings to a plan or design for new or substantially improved products/processes before commercial production (prototypes, pilot plants). IAS 38.57 requires capitalisation once ALL criteria are met:
lines: Intention to complete and use or sell
Adequate technical, financial and other resources
steps.result: Development costs → intangible asset once the criteria are met

steps.title: Impact on profit
steps.why: Research hits profit immediately. Capitalised development is amortised from market launch over its useful life, so profit is reduced gradually.
steps.result: Expense now (research) vs amortisation over time (development)

pitfalls: Saying that all R&D can be capitalised – research never can.
Saying development is optional to capitalise: if all criteria are met, IAS 38 requires it.

prompt: Explain the criteria that distinguish a lease from a service contract under IFRS 16.
modelAnswer: A contract is (or contains) a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. Three tests: (1) identified asset – explicitly or implicitly specified, with no substantive substitution right of the supplier; (2) the customer has the right to obtain substantially all economic benefits from its use; (3) the customer has the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used (or these decisions are predetermined and the customer operates or designed the asset). In a service contract the supplier keeps control of the asset used to deliver the service. The distinction matters because service contracts are expensed, leases are recognised on the balance sheet (ROU asset + liability).
keyPoints: Identified asset, no substantive substitution right
Right to substantially all economic benefits
Right to direct how and for what purpose it is used
Service: supplier controls the asset; lease → on balance sheet

steps.title: Start from the IFRS 16 definition
steps.why: A contract is (or contains) a lease if it conveys the right to CONTROL the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration.

steps.title: Test 1 – identified asset
steps.why: The asset is specified explicitly or implicitly, and the supplier has NO substantive substitution right (i.e. it cannot practically and profitably swap the asset). Example: retail unit that the owner can relocate at any time at minimal cost → no identified asset.

steps.title: Test 2 – economic benefits
steps.why: The customer obtains substantially all economic benefits from using the asset during the period.

steps.title: Test 3 – right to direct the use
steps.why: The customer decides how and for what purpose the asset is used (or these decisions are predetermined and the customer operates/designed it). Example: lessor must approve truck routes each quarter → the customer does not direct the use.

steps.title: Consequence
steps.why: All three tests met → lease: right-of-use asset + lease liability on the balance sheet. Otherwise → service contract: the supplier keeps control and the payments are expensed.
steps.result: Lease = identified asset + benefits + right to direct; otherwise service

pitfalls: Looking only at the contract's name ('rental', 'service') instead of the control tests.

prompt: Lecture cases 6 and 7: (1) BRAND rents Retail Unit A for 5 years; the owner may relocate BRAND to a similar unit but must pay the relocation costs; BRAND decides on assortment, prices and stock and controls access. (2) SAUSAGE rents 'a space' for 3 years that the operator may move at any time at minimal cost; many suitable areas exist. Lease or service contract?
modelAnswer: (1) Lease: Retail Unit A is an identified asset – the owner's substitution right is not substantive because relocation is costly for him (he pays BRAND's costs); BRAND obtains substantially all benefits and directs the use. The cleaning/security/advertising services are non-lease components. (2) Service contract: the operator has a substantive substitution right (practical ability to move SAUSAGE at any time, many alternative areas, minimal cost, benefits from relocating) → no identified asset → payments expensed.
keyPoints: Case 2: substantive substitution right → service contract

steps.title: Apply the IFRS 16 tests
lines: 2. Customer gets substantially all economic benefits?
3. Customer directs how and for what purpose the asset is used?

steps.title: BRAND – Retail Unit A
steps.why: A substitution right is only substantive if the supplier can practically substitute AND benefits economically. Here the owner must provide a similar unit and pay BRAND's relocation costs → no economic benefit → not substantive. BRAND decides on assortment, prices, stock and controls access → directs the use.
steps.result: Lease (services like cleaning/security are separate non-lease components)

steps.title: SAUSAGE – a space in the building
steps.why: The operator can move SAUSAGE at any time, many suitable areas exist, costs are minimal and relocating helps him use the space best → substantive substitution right → no identified asset.

prompt: A local industrial company has developed a prototype that can recover wind energy together with a foreign partner. Commercialisation is doubtful: the selling price needed to cover manufacturing costs would be too high for potential buyers. These prototype development costs …

options.text: will be capitalised because the project is identifiable and controlled by the company
will be capitalised because the project is controlled, the costs can be measured reliably and future profits will be shared between the partners
will be expensed as there is no expectation of future profits
will be expensed because future profits will be shared between the two partners

explanation: IAS 38: development costs are capitalised only if ALL criteria are met – including the ability to generate probable future economic benefits (a market / commercial viability). Without expected profits the costs are expensed. Sharing profits with a partner is irrelevant.
